summary:
Section 162 of the Kenyan Penal Code makes carnal knowledge against the order of nature a felony punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, rising to 21 years where the act is committed without consent or where consent is obtained by force, threats, fear of bodily harm or false representations as to the nature of the act. Section 163 punishes an attempt with 7 years, and section 165 punishes acts of gross indecency between males with 5 years. On 24 May 2019 the High Court declined to declare sections 162 and 165 unconstitutional in Eric Gitari v Attorney General (Petition 150 of 2016); a Court of Appeal hearing was scheduled for May 2026 and no decision is recorded in this inventory.

Kenya has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition, and no statute provides a legal means to change gender. Evidence before the Milimani High Court in Nairobi (Justice Bahati Mwamuye, Petition 27 of 2020, decision delivered 20 May 2026) showed that 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans were refused by civil registration offices, with some spending nearly four years' wages on failed document corrections. That court ruled on 20 May 2026 that Kenyans must be allowed to change gender markers on identification documents, in a suit filed by transgender activist Audrey Mbugua and two others seeking to amend birth certificates.

On 12 August 2025 the Eldoret High Court found that a trans Kenyan petitioner's rights, including freedom from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, equality and non-discrimination, dignity, freedom and security of the person, and privacy, were violated during incarceration, where she had been subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered 'gender determination'. The court directed the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act, or in the alternative amend the Intersex Persons Bill 2024, finding that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections. No legislation enacted in response is recorded in this inventory.

Intersex people are legally recognised as a third gender. No Kenyan statute governs gender identity or provides a codified pathway for legal gender change. Article 45(2) of the Constitution, effective 27 August 2010, authorises only opposite-sex marriage, and the state recognises no same-sex relationships; a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no legal standing for that partnership. The Children Act 2001 makes homosexual and unmarried couples ineligible to adopt. There are no explicit statutory protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, though Article 27(4)-(5) non-discrimination provisions have been argued to allow claims on sexual orientation grounds, an interpretation the government accepted in a May 2012 UN submission.

Police harassment of trans and gender-nonconforming people is documented. A CNN 'A Equals' interactive drawing on 26 interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi describes routine police detention on pretexts such as 'drunk and disorderly' and on-the-spot extortion, with officers demanding 5,000 shillings; interviewees use traditionally male names as pseudonyms to move through public space. The Kenya Human Rights Commission (2011) and the National Gay and Lesbian Human Rights Commission (2020-2021) reported routine police harassment, detention in remand beyond the constitutional period without charges, presentation on trumped-up charges, extortion and blackmail for bribes, demands for bribes and sexual favours from men who have sex with men sex workers, and rape by state security officers. The most recent documented instance of such abuse in this inventory is the 2025 Eldoret High Court petition; no later case is recorded.

The Kenya Human Rights Commission's 'Lives on the Line' report (September 2025), built with more than 14 community organisations, is the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering October 2023 to September 2024. It explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling (Petition 16/2019) that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence. The report's sampling was purposive, drawn from organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision, so its figures describe documented cases rather than prevalence.

A Kenyan man was sentenced to 50 years' imprisonment in December 2024 for killing an LGBTQ activist; this is the most recent documented killing of an LGBTQ person in this inventory, and no later instance is recorded. The inventory contains no trans-specific killing rate for Kenya and no general homicide rate for comparison, so no trans-specific magnitude can be stated.

Court-driven protections have expanded over the past decade. The Court of Appeal in Mombasa ruled on 22 March 2018 that forced anal examinations on persons accused of same-sex relations are unconstitutional, reversing a 2016 High Court decision; the case arose from police arrests in February 2015 of two men in Kwale County who were subjected to forced anal examinations, HIV and hepatitis B tests at Mombasa's Madaraka Hospital, and a later anal examination was halted by the Kangundo magistrate court for two men taken from Kakuyuni to Kangundo Level 4 hospital. Compensation in that matter was awarded in 2024. In 2023 the Supreme Court upheld freedom of association, allowing LGBTQ organisation registration.

The Family Protection Bill (file DLS/NA/BILLS/2/18/2023), introduced in 2023 by MP George Peter Opondo Kaluma, would punish 'aggravated homosexuality' with death, criminalise promotion of LGBTQ+ activity, restrict privacy, assembly and public demonstration, prohibit pride parades, provide for monitoring of private and public spaces, remove LGBTQ+ topics from school curricula, and overturn the 2023 Supreme Court association decision. The bill has remained stalled before the Committee on Social Protection for close to two years; it is not law.

Trans people face documented barriers to gender-affirming care. A Kenya National Commission on Human Rights report of April 2012 recorded a witness who completed all required processes but was declined surgery by Kenyatta National Hospital without reasons, with an appeal to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentist's Board unsuccessful. The same report states police face difficulties deciding whether to detain transgender individuals in male or female cells when arrested, and that transgender people fear using sex-designated bathrooms in entertainment areas for fear of being accused of using bathrooms for sexual crimes. It also records that when a partner discovers a transgender person's sex status, the partner's reaction can attract a public crowd, exposing the transgender person to stigma and public nuisance accusations.

LGBTI civil-society groups may operate but only within a restrictive civic space, per the UK Home Office country policy note of February 2025. The US State Department Human Rights Report for the 2010 reporting year recorded that LGBT advocacy organisations such as the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya were permitted to register and operate, that societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread causing loss of employment and education, and that in February 2010 Mtwapa religious leaders demanded closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute. In 2010-2012 ICCPR and Universal Periodic Review responses the Kenyan government stated it would not decriminalise same-sex unions as taboo and culturally unacceptable, while stating it did not support discrimination in access to services including HIV/AIDS prevention under the 2006 Act.
tangentialFactors:
The Kenyan legal landscape on sexual orientation and gender identity is shaped by litigation rather than legislation: the 2018 forced-anal-examination ruling, the 2023 association decision, the August 2025 Eldoret trans-rights judgment and the May 2026 gender-marker ruling all came from the courts, while Parliament has produced no implementing statute and the Family Protection Bill moves in the opposite direction.

Kenya's recognition of intersex people as a third gender, without any framework for transgender people, creates an asymmetry: a gender-nonconforming visitor may find intersex recognition discussed in official documents while trans identity remains outside the legal vocabulary.

Documentation of violations is improving. The KHRC 'Lives on the Line' report of September 2025 is described as the first comprehensive documentation of its kind, covering October 2023 to September 2024 and built with more than 14 community organisations; its purposive sampling means it captures reported cases rather than population prevalence.

Kenya's government has, in international forums, simultaneously declined to decriminalise same-sex relations and affirmed non-discrimination in access to services including HIV/AIDS prevention, a split posture that shapes what a visitor can expect from official statements versus official practice.
